Left: hub touches every edge, so is_vertex_cover() returns True. Right: the leaf a alone leaves the edges hub-b and hub-c (shown in the accent color) untouched, so is_vertex_cover() returns False." width="100%"} A vertex cover is a set of nodes such that every edge has at least one endpoint in the set. It is the complement of an independent set: a set of nodes is a vertex cover exactly when the remaining nodes have no edges among them. Use this method to validate the output of `bipartite_vertex_cover()` or `minimum_weighted_vertex_cover()`, or a hand-picked set of monitors. Edge direction is ignored, and a self-loop is only covered by its own node. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A list of node IDs or labels. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if every edge has an endpoint in `nodes`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} One pass over the edge list in $O(V + E)$ time. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The center of a star covers every edge; any leaves alone do not: ::: {#53e3b3a6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["hub", "a", "b", "c"]) g.add_edges([("hub", "a"), ("hub", "b"), ("hub", "c")]) g.is_vertex_cover(["hub"]), g.is_vertex_cover(["a", "b", "c"]), g.is_vertex_cover(["a"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, True, False) ``` ::: :::
